items.headline: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
items.blurb: Moscow says it is "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump says the world is "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
items.text: Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war. Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said. The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader. Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles. Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been." items.headline: Colombian president purges National Museum of works promoting ‘communism’
items.blurb: Far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella says he will wage a 'counterrevolution' against cultural institutions.
items.text: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has announced he is spearheading a cultural “counterrevolution” that includes removing dozens of exhibits from the National Museum, drawing protests and comparisons to United States President Donald Trump. De la Espriella, a conservative Trump ally , said last week that he wants to prevent cultural institutions from being taken over by what he calls “atheist social communism”. Since then, exhibits have been taken down that once addressed the history of social movements, including feminist and LGBTQ+ activism, and Colombia’s political violence. The changes have sparked protests by civil rights groups, artists and students who have accused the government of censorship and warn that important parts of the country’s history could be erased. Dozens of demonstrators gathered on Wednesday outside the National Museum in downtown Bogota as riot police guarded its entrance. “I find it outrageous that they want to erase part of our history,” said Azul Riascos, a history student. items.text: Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’ The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday. It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.” The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week. The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation. “The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical. items.headline: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
items.blurb: President Vladimir Putin does not feel under pressure right now to end the war, the BBC's Russia Editor writes.
items.text: After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending? "Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives. In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting. But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow. The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level. In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..." items.text: Neil Bush, brother of former Republican President George W Bush, has said that he voted for the Democratic candidate James Talarico in a crucial race for the United States Senate. In a social media post on Tuesday, Bush said he voted for Talarico due to concerns about the Republican candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton . Talarico and Paxton are in a tight race for Texas’s open Senate seat. Democrats are hoping to seize control of the 100-member Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, when 35 seats will be on the ballot. Bush’s endorsement of Talarico is the latest sign of division among Texas Republicans. Bush comes from a prominent Republican family: not only was his brother a president, but his father, the late George HW Bush, was too. “My concerns about his judgment and conduct are hardly mine alone,” Bush wrote. “He was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House, although subsequently acquitted by the Texas Senate.” To explain his decision, Bush pointed to Paxton’s divisive track record, including efforts to support President Donald Trump’s false claims about the

items.headline: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
items.blurb: The comment is an apparent swipe at Benjamin Netanyahu and Donald Trump, who both face elections in coming weeks.
items.text: French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes. Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests. Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic". It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month. Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots. Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice. items.headline: One killed, eight injured in attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd airport
items.blurb: Injured immediately transported to hospitals as aviation authority says updates will be forthcoming.
items.text: One person has been killed and eight injured in an attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam, the country’s civil aviation authority announced. All of the wounded, whose injuries range from minor to critical, were transported to hospitals to receive medical attention, the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Wednesday. Earlier in the day, two people were killed after Saudi air defences intercepted a drone that was attempting to hit a facility at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield, the Ministry of Energy said. It was the latest in a series of assaults on Saudi airports as conflict intensifies between Houthi forces and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised Yemeni government. Last week, the kingdom reported that a projectile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 11 killed one person and injured 11. On October 10, the civil aviation authority reported that a separate attack on the same airport claimed the lives of 12 people and injured more than 300. items.headline: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
items.blurb: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.
items.text: Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said. The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country. The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said. Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality. “Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement.

items.headline: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
items.blurb: Test results have confirmed his diagnosis as a lung adenocarcinoma that was localised.
items.text: Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said. Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican. "A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added. The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds. It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday. The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung. items.headline: Courts can’t suggest custodial quizzing, says Supreme Court
items.blurb: The order is significant for the distinction it draws between the investigating agency’s discretion in deciding the manner of interrogation.
items.text: Courts cannot suggest to investigating agencies that an accused or suspect should be subjected to custodial interrogation, the Supreme Court has held, cautioning that sweeping observations on the need to take people into custody can jeopardise their liberty. A bench of justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar underlined it is for the investigating agency to seek custodial interrogation or otherwise, and not for courts to suggest or dictate the nature of custody or questioning required in a case. “We are of the firm view that it is not for the high court to suggest any form of interrogation of an accused. This should be best left to the discretion of the investigating agency,” said the bench in a recent order, while adding that any “sweeping observation” about the custody of other accused or suspects in the case ought to be avoided. The order is significant for the distinction it draws between the investigating agency’s discretion in deciding the manner of interrogation and a court’s role while considering a plea for protection from arrest. items.headline: ‘Won’t call Jantar Mantar stir’: CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka released after 7-day custody based on condition
items.blurb: The SEM directed Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to furnish personal bonds and sureties of ₹50,000 each and appear for a hearing on October 23.
items.text: A special executive magistrate on Wednesday ordered the release of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka from judicial custody after they agreed not to call any protests at Jantar Mantar until the site is re-notified as a designated protest site. The written undertakings, furnished before assistant commissioner of police (ACP) Ritu Raj, acting as the SEM of New Delhi district , said, “We reiterate our undertaking and commitment towards peace, law and order, public tranquility and further we specifically state that we will not make any calls for protest at Jantar Mantar till such a time that it is de-notified in accordance with law.” In it, they also promised “not to commit any breach of peace” and expressed “full faith” in the judiciary and the SEM court. The undertakings further reiterated that any protest undertaken by them would be done “within the four corners of the constitution”. The order was also made public on Wednesday. The court thereby, accepted the undertakings and ordered their release on furnishing personal bonds and surety bonds of ₹ 50,000 each.

items.text: A New Mexico court ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data. This came as one of the largest financial penalties imposed on a company in US history. According to Reuters , the case stems from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict, Reuters reported. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion. items.text: After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund. Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund. A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks. It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go? It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time. "The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said. items.headline: Ex-Brevan Howard Trader Sued by Quant Who Joined His New Fund
items.blurb: Ex-Brevan Howard Asset Management portfolio manager Robert Sicari was accused of withholding millions of dollars in promised trading profits from a former colleague who joined his new fund.
items.text: (Bloomberg) -- Ex-Brevan Howard Asset Management portfolio manager Robert Sicari was accused of withholding millions of dollars in promised trading profits from a former colleague who joined his new fund. Wooyoung Hong, who worked under Sicari at Brevan Howard as a quantitative researcher, said in a complaint filed Tuesday in New York that they were both fired from that firm in 2024. Sicari subsequently approached Hong about joining ThirtyPark Capital, the fund he was starting to invest his own money, according to the suit. Hong claims Sicari promised to pay him 50% of the gains from certain trades and give him a 30% stake in ThirtyPark. In his suit, Hong estimates that he’s entitled to as much as $3.5 million for trades he handled from November 2024 to December 2025 but says Sicari kept the money to try to force him to renegotiate the equity portion of their deal. Reached Tuesday, Sicari had no immediate comment beyond saying that ThirtyPark is no longer operating. He didn’t reply to follow-up messages on Wednesday. A lawyer for Sicari declined to comment. items.text: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history. A 4–1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future. He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4–1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later. However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards. items.headline: Jansen takes five for South Africa as Australia forced to follow on
items.text: Marco Jansen took five wickets as Australia crashed to 99 all out in reply to South Africa's first innings of 425–9 declared on the fourth day of the second Test at St George's Park on Wednesday (October 23, 2026). With a first innings lead of 326 runs, South Africa enforced the follow-on despite fast bowler Anrich Nortje being out of action with a groin injury. Tall left-armer Jansen struck with his first ball of the innings when he had nightwatchman Scott Boland caught behind in the second over of the day. He followed up with the wickets of Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Alex Carey and Beau Webster as Australia collapsed. Steve Smith, who twice needed treatment for what appeared to be a neck injury, top-scored for Australia with 28 before being bowled by Wiaan Mulder. items.headline: Suma Shirur unveils Axis Bank Lakshya Shooting Club HPC
items.text: The red state transport bus that once took Suma Shirur from Panvel to Dadar and beyond for practice has come to symbolise how far the Olympian has travelled in her pursuit of creating a better ecosystem for Indian shooters. Twenty years after starting the Lakshya Shooting Club, Shirur on Wednesday unveiled the Axis Bank Lakshya Shooting Club High Performance Centre in Belapur. Olympic medallist Gagan Narang inaugurated the seven-storied facility in the presence of six other Olympians and several shooting stalwarts. Equipped with two modern shooting ranges, a sports science laboratory, a gym, a mind gym, a Pilates studio, residential accommodation and a lounge, the centre is designed as a one-stop destination for aspiring shooters. Supported by Axis Bank and the Government of Maharashtra, it aims to provide athletes with the infrastructure and expertise needed to compete at the highest level. “Like all the Olympians from my generation will agree, we never had access to anything. We only saw others using it and wished we had the same,” Shirur said. “I would like to create things that I never got.”

items.headline: The new economics of enterprise AI
items.blurb: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious.
items.text: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from "can we use it?" to "how efficiently are we using it?" Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes. That's the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow. items.headline: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
items.blurb: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line.
items.text: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn't a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie. Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1). items.headline: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
items.blurb: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
items.text: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. items.headline: Judge rejects Trump’s wild claim EPA can dismiss data center pollution lawsuits
items.blurb: Trump’s EPA can't unilaterally dismiss SpaceXAI pollution lawsuit, court rules.
items.text: Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI is stuck facing a lawsuit over alleged data center pollution after Donald Trump failed to convince a judge that his Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has complete control over all Clean Air Act lawsuits and can dismiss any suit at whim. Soon after unpermitted gas turbines were discovered powering Musk’s giant Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, the NAACP sued . Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI (which, following a merger , is known now as SpaceXAI) to use the best available pollution control technology when operating the turbines and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. Without such remedies, the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby, the NAACP argued. To block the lawsuit, Trump tried to intervene, arguing that the EPA had the power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. items.blurb: Meta changes AI scraping policy but won’t add language respecting robots.txt.
items.text: Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30. Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout.
